groundTruthNotes.repository: https://github.com/TriLinder/OpenTapasReader (Capacitor-based; if Cordova bridge is present at runtime it is the standard framework code from apache/cordova-android)
groundTruthNotes.analysis: The three @JavascriptInterface methods are thin delegators to CordovaBridge.jsExec/jsRetrieveJsMessages/jsSetNativeToJsBridgeMode. ALL THREE FIRST CALL verifySecret(bridgeSecret) — a SecureRandom-generated int that JavaScript must possess to make the call succeed; mismatch returns null/false and disables the bridge (throwing IllegalAccessException). The secret is delivered to JS at cordova.js initialization, so same-origin app JS has it automatically; cross-origin or injected JS does NOT (unless XSS in trusted content or allowNavigation misconfiguration). exec() routes to PluginManager.exec(service, action, callbackId, arguments), which dispatches to plugins REGISTERED IN config.xml — NOT to Runtime.exec, NOT to a shell, NOT to arbitrary reflection on arbitrary classes. retrieveJsMessages() pops responses from NativeToJsMessageQueue that native plugins enqueued — the data flow is native-to-JS (queue drain), not JS-to-native exfiltration. setNativeToJsBridgeMode() only switches between POLL / ONLINE_EVENTS / EVAL bridge modes. The correct framework-level findings would be: (1) exec() is a high-reach plugin-dispatch surface whose effective security depends on which plugins are registered AND on bridge-secret protection AND on the WebView's content-origin policy; (2) the EVAL bridge mode does call evaluateJavascript on JS the native side composed, which is fine because the native side controls it. Pure-framework SQL injection, framework Runtime.exec RCE, framework path-traversal, PII from setNativeToJsBridgeMode, and Intent Redirection via integer-only setters are NOT possible. Every inspector missed the bridge-secret mitigation — a meaningful blind spot.

researcherConclusion._methodology: Ground truth: The three bridge methods are thin delegators to CordovaBridge methods, each gated by verifySecret(bridgeSecret). exec() routes to PluginManager.exec which dispatches to plugins registered in config.xml — it does NOT call Runtime.exec, does NOT touch SQL, does NOT directly construct Intents or file paths in framework code, and does NOT use unbounded reflection. retrieveJsMessages() pops native-enqueued plugin responses; setNativeToJsBridgeMode() switches between POLL/ONLINE_EVENTS/EVAL message-delivery modes. The legitimate framework-level concerns are: exec is the central plugin-dispatch surface (impact bounded by registered plugins); reflection-based plugin instantiation is constrained to config.xml entries; bridge-secret protection MUST be acknowledged for any reachability claim. The largest collective failure across all inspectors is that NONE mentioned verifySecret/bridgeSecret — a substantive blind spot. Each auditor is judged on whether it correctly rewards/penalizes the inspectors' relative quality: gemma3 produced the most cautious and architecturally-grounded findings (partials, no fabrications), phi4 was the most conservative (3 findings, 2 partials, 1 invalid), qwen produced massive looping garbage (130+ findings, mostly fabricated and repeated), llama3.2 produced fabricated code snippets and self-contradicting findings, deepseek produced one closest-to-truth reflection finding amid several fabrications, and starcoder produced nothing. A good auditor should score gemma3 and phi4 highest, qwen and llama3.2 lowest, and starcoder zero-or-NA.
